title: Intrinsic Fluorescence as a Probe of Structural Dynamics and Interactions of Human Adenovirus with Surfactants and Liposomes
abstract: In this work, the intrinsic fluorescence of Human Adenovirus serotype 2 (HAdV-2), arising from tryptophan (Trp) and tyrosine (Tyr) residues present in viral proteins, was used to monitor structural changes in the three-dimensional organization of the viral particle as a function of the inactivation method employed (UV irradiation or paraformaldehyde (PFA) treatment), temperature, and the presence of negatively and positively charged surfactants. Steady-state fluorescence anisotropy was used to investigate the interaction between HAdV-2 and zwitterionic or negatively charged liposomes by monitoring both the extrinsic fluorescent probe 1,6-diphenyl-1,3,5-hexatriene (DPH) inserted into the lipid bilayer and the intrinsic anisotropy of Trp residues from viral proteins. Tyr fluorescence emission proved to be more sensitive to temperature variations, whereas Trp emission was more strongly affected in samples inactivated with PFA. In the presence of surfactants, stronger interactions were observed with negatively charged micelles, resulting in enhanced Tyr fluorescence and quenched Trp fluorescence. The most pronounced effect was observed for the interaction between HAdV-2 and negatively charged 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol), sodium salt (DPPG) liposomes. In the presence of viral particles, the phase transition temperature (Tm) of DPPG liposomes increased by approximately 11 °C, while no detectable structural changes were observed in the three-dimensional organization of the viral particle itself. Overall, these results highlight intrinsic fluorescence as a valuable approach for probing the structural organization of HAdV-2 under different environmental and interfacial conditions.

title: Single-Cell BCR and Transcriptome Analysis Revealed Potent Neutralizing Antibodies in Response to HAdV-4 Infection
abstract: Human adenovirus type 4 (HAdV-4) is a predominant serotype causing acute respiratory infections, for which no antibody drugs have been clinically approved to date, resulting in an urgent unmet medical need. This study aimed to identify highly potent neutralizing antibodies by dissecting the B cell immune response after infection, thereby laying a foundation for vaccine design and antiviral therapy. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from a convalescent patient who exhibited the most robust neutralizing antibody titers among 16 HAdV-4 convalescent volunteers. A total of 2710 B cells were isolated from the peripheral blood of this patient, and the characteristics of B cell subsets and B cell receptor (BCR) repertoires were comprehensively analyzed by integrating scRNA-seq and scVDJ-seq technologies. Candidate antibodies were subsequently selected for a series of functional and mechanistic validations based on the characteristics of BCRs and origination. Transcriptomic profiling classified memory B cells into three functionally heterogeneous subpopulations designated as MB sub1, sub2 and sub3. Combined with the characteristics of BCR, 92 selected antibodies from sub2 and sub3 were synthesized for further functional validation. Three potent neutralizing antibodies were successfully identified, among which 1QH7 demonstrated potentially potent virus neutralization capability in vitro and conferred robust in vivo protection in the Stat1-deficient mouse model. We further employed AlphaFold 3 to predict the complex structure of 1QH7 with the HAdV-4 Hexon protein and validated the key binding residues through site-directed mutagenesis. Additionally, the study elucidated the viral neutralization mechanism mediated by TRIM21. We established an efficient antibody screening strategy based on integration of scRNA-seq and scVDJ-seq and isolated a potent neutralizing antibody, 1QH7. This study lays a solid foundation for the rapid pathogen-bait-free, cell subset-guided screening antibody route for novel emerging infectious disease outbreaks.

title: Assessment of the Necessity for High-Level Disinfection (HLD) of Reusable Ophthalmic Devices: A Multisociety Position Paper.
abstract: Regulatory agencies in the United States and abroad are increasingly citing clinics and surgical facilities for what they deem to be inadequate disinfection of Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) tips, gonioscopy lenses, laser lenses, and other reusable clinic devices that contact the ocular surface. These regulators require routine high-level disinfection (HLD) of these reusable devices to prevent infection transmission. A multisociety task force formed to assess the necessity of HLD found no published evidence that these devices transmit sight-threatening infections or that HLD reduces infection transmission compared with lower-level disinfection methods. Meanwhile, routine use of chemical HLD reduces clinic efficiency, increases healthcare costs and waste, and may damage device surfaces potentially affecting patient care. Underlying these mandates for HLD is the nearly century-old Spaulding classification system, which inappropriately groups the ocular surface with heavily contaminated mucous membranes. A task force survey with more than 1000 ophthalmologist respondents found that the most common reprocessing methods were alcohol wiping for GAT tips and either alcohol wiping or soap and water for diagnostic or laser lenses. Many respondents using chemical HLD reported adverse effects, including ocular surface chemical toxicity and device damage. Despite infrequent use of HLD, reported infection transmission was exceedingly rare and generally limited to self-limited adenoviral conjunctivitis. The task force agreed with the majority (88%) of ophthalmologists surveyed that HLD should not be required for these reusable devices in routine clinical care. Instead, HLD should be a discretionary consideration in higher-risk circumstances, such as following use of these devices in patients with suspected infection. This paper presents the summary recommendations of a policy statement approved by the American Academy of Ophthalmology Board of Trustees and endorsed by four subspecialty societies.

full_text: IntroductionHuman adenovirus type 3 (HAdV-3) is a major adenovirus type associated with respiratory infections in China. Despite its clinical importance, the biological characteristics and potential biomedical applications of contemporary circulating HAdV-3 strains remain incompletely understood. Naturally occurring species B adenoviruses also remain relatively underexplored as potential starting backbones for oncolytic virotherapy. This study aimed to characterize a contemporary clinical HAdV-3 isolate and evaluate its viral genome amplification, apoptosis induction, and antitumor activity.MethodsA clinical HAdV-3 isolate, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, was recovered from a throat swab specimen from a patient with adenovirus-associated respiratory disease. Viral identity and genomic characteristics were determined using multiplex PCR, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and recombination analysis. Viral genome amplification kinetics were evaluated in human respiratory-related and tumor-derived cell lines and a murine cell line by quantitative PCR. Comparative apoptosis induction by HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 was assessed in 293F cells infected at a low multiplicity of infection using Annexin V/PI flow cytometry. Antitumor activity was evaluated following repeated intratumoral administration of HAdV-3-TZ01 in an A549-luciferase xenograft model in BALB/c-nu nude mice, with tumor growth and bioluminescence monitored longitudinally.ResultsGenomic and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that HAdV-3-TZ01 belonged to HAdV-3 within species B and exhibited a genomic backbone highly conserved with contemporary circulating HAdV-3 strains. A short putative HAdV-7-derived recombinant fragment was identified. HAdV-3-TZ01 showed efficient viral genome amplification in multiple human respiratory-related cell lines, including A549, H3122, BEAS-2B, MRC-5, and HEK293FT cells, whereas genome amplification was markedly restricted in murine L929 cells. HAdV-3-TZ01 induced a significantly higher proportion of late apoptotic cells than HAdV-5 in 293F cells under low-multiplicity infection conditions, although the absolute increase in total apoptosis was modest. In the A549-luciferase xenograft model, intratumoral administration of HAdV-3-TZ01 significantly suppressed tumor progression. By day 43, mean tumor volume was reduced by approximately 54% and tumor-associated bioluminescence by approximately 50% compared with mock-treated controls. No significant body-weight loss or overt signs of distress were observed under the experimental conditions.ConclusionHAdV-3-TZ01 retains the characteristic human epithelial tropism of HAdV-3 and exhibits efficient viral genome amplification in human epithelial-derived cells, apoptosis induction, and measurable antitumor activity in vivo. The apoptosis difference between HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 should be interpreted cautiously because the analysis was limited to 293F cells and did not establish a tumor-specific pro-apoptotic mechanism. As an unmodified respiratory pathogen, HAdV-3-TZ01 should not be considered a directly translatable therapeutic agent. Rather, these findings support HAdV-3-TZ01 as a potential starting backbone for future genetic engineering aimed at improving tumor selectivity and safety. 2Materials and methods2.1Cells and virusesHEK293FT, A549, BEAS-2B, H3122, MRC-5, and L929 cell lines were maintained in our laboratory. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (#BC-M-005, BioChannel, China) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (#BC-SE-FBS07, BioChannel, China) at 37 °C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO2. HEK293FT cells (an adherent derivative of HEK293 expressing the SV40 large T antigen) were used for virus propagation and TCID50 titration. 293F cells (a suspension-adapted derivative of HEK293 maintained in serum-free medium) were used exclusively for apoptosis analysis. Both cell lines are derived from human embryonic kidney cells and are not tumor-derived. The suspension growth characteristics of 293F cells facilitate uniform cell preparation and flow cytometric analysis. HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 used in the comparative apoptosis assay were propagated and titrated using the same HEK293FT cell system to ensure consistency of viral preparations. Wild-type human adenovirus type 5 (HAdV-5) was obtained from Guangzhou Paizhen Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (#WRS-240802, Guangzhou, China). The HAdV-3 isolate used in this study, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, was isolated from a clinical throat swab specimen and propagated in HEK293FT cells before characterization and subsequent experiments.2.2Clinical sample collection and virus isolationA throat swab specimen was collected from a 5-year-old female patient admitted to The Affiliated Taizhou People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, Taizhou, China, on May 23, 2024. The patient presented with fever and cough for 4 days before admission. Respiratory pathogen testing revealed adenovirus DNA positivity, and chest radiography indicated bronchopneumonia. The specimen was collected during hospitalization for adenovirus isolation and further characterization. Samples were transported on ice and processed within 12 h after collection. The specimen was diluted 1:1 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), clarified by centrifugation at 1,500 × g for 10 min, and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. The filtrate was supplemented with penicillin (100 IU/mL) and streptomycin (100 μg/mL) before inoculation.HEK293FT cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. For virus isolation, confluent HEK293FT cell monolayers were inoculated with clarified clinical specimens and incubated for 2 h to allow viral adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, fresh maintenance medium containing 2% FBS was added. Cells were monitored daily for cytopathic effects (CPE). Blind passaging was performed every 5–7 days in the absence of visible CPE. Virus-containing supernatants were harvested following the appearance of characteristic adenoviral CPE, clarified by low-speed centrifugation, aliquoted, and stored at −80 °C. Third-passage (P3) virus stocks were used for subsequent experiments.For in vivo administration, the P3 virus stock was concentrated by sucrose cushion ultracentrifugation. Briefly, virus-containing supernatants together with infected cell pellets were subjected to three cycles of freeze–thaw (−80 °C/37 °C) to release intracellular viral particles, followed by low-speed centrifugation (3,000 × g, 4 °C, 20 min) to remove cellular debris. The clarified supernatant was layered onto a 20% sucrose cushion prepared in PBS (pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 100,000 × g for 2 h at 4 °C. The viral pellet was resuspended in sterile PBS and stored at −80 °C. The resulting concentrated virus stock was used for subsequent in vivo experiments. The viral titer was determined by TCID50 assay as described below, yielding 3.16 × 1011 TCID50/mL.2.3Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysisTransmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was performed by Shanghai Weishi Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Briefly, 5 μL of virus-enriched sample was placed onto a Formvar–carbon-coated copper grid and incubated for 5 min, followed by blotting with filter paper. The samples were fixed with 1% glutaraldehyde (final concentration) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) for 1 min. After washing with phosphate buffer, the grids were negatively stained with 1% uranyl acetate. Images were acquired using a transmission electron microscope (Talos 120, FEI, USA) according to standard operating procedures.2.4Virus titration by TCID50 assayVirus infectivity was determined by a tissue culture infectious dose 50% (TCID50) assay in 293FT cells. Briefly, 293FT cells were seeded into 96-well plates at 1 × 104 cells per well and cultured overnight. Virus stocks were serially diluted 10-fold in DMEM containing 2% FBS, and 100 μL of each dilution was added to eight replicate wells. After incubation at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere, the wells were monitored daily for the appearance of cytopathic effects (CPE). CPE-positive and CPE-negative wells were recorded at 3 days post-infection, and viral titers were calculated using the Reed–Muench method and expressed as TCID50/mL.2.5Viral identification and whole-genome sequencingViral DNA was extracted from infected-cell culture supernatants using a Universal Genomic DNA Kit (#CW2298M, Cowin Biotech Co., Ltd., China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Preliminary species identification was performed using a previously described multiplex PCR assay targeting conserved regions of the adenoviral hexon gene (Xu et al., 2000). PCR products were purified and subjected to Sanger sequencing. Consensus sequences were compared against the NCBI nucleotide database using BLAST for preliminary virus typing.For whole-genome characterization, viral genomic DNA was submitted to a commercial sequencing service provider for next-generation sequencing. Sequencing libraries were prepared according to standard protocols and sequenced using paired-end 150-bp reads on an Illumina NovaSeq platform. Raw sequencing reads were subjected to quality control and de novo assembly to obtain the complete viral genome sequence. Open reading frames were annotated based on sequence homology with representative adenovirus reference genomes available in GenBank.2.6Phylogenetic and recombination analysesRepresentative human adenovirus reference sequences were retrieved from GenBank. Multiple sequence alignments were generated using MEGA version 11 (Tamura et al., 2021). The optimal nucleotide substitution model was selected using the “Find Best DNA/Protein Models” function implemented in MEGA. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using the maximum-likelihood method with 1,000 bootstrap replicates.Potential recombination events were identified using RDP4 (v4.101) with multiple detection algorithms under default settings (Martin et al., 2015). Putative recombination signals were further evaluated using SimPlot (v3.5.1) based on similarity plot and bootscanning analyses (Lole et al., 1999).2.7Comparative apoptosis analysis293F cells (a suspension-adapted derivative of HEK293 maintained in serum-free medium) were used for this assay. This cell line was chosen because its suspension growth characteristics facilitate uniform cell preparation and high-throughput flow cytometric analysis, which is technically advantageous for detecting subtle differences in apoptotic populations. Cells were cultured in Trans CD05 medium (#YYCD05, Youyi Biotechnology, China) at 37 °C with 5% CO2 in a shaking incubator (125 rpm). Cells were infected with HAdV-3 or HAdV-5 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.001. HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 used in this comparative assay were propagated and titrated using the same HEK293FT cell system to ensure consistency of viral preparations. Following infection, cell samples were collected at 48 h post-infection for apoptosis analysis.Apoptosis was assessed using an Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (#C1062M, Beyotime, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed once with cold PBS, and resuspended in Annexin V binding buffer. Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI) were added sequentially, and samples were incubated for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. Flow cytometric analysis was performed using a CaleCyter2080 flow cytometer (Calerio, China). At least 10,000 events were acquired for each sample.Data were analyzed using FlowJo V10 software. Viable cells, early apoptotic cells (Annexin V+/PI−), and late apoptotic cells (Annexin V+/PI+) were quantified. Total apoptosis was defined as the sum of early and late apoptotic populations. All experiments were performed in three independent biological replicates.2.8Cell tropism and viral genome amplificationHuman lung carcinoma A549 cells, human bronchial epithelial BEAS-2B cells, human lung adenocarcinoma H3122 cells, human lung fibroblast MRC-5 cells, human embryonic kidney 293FT cells, and murine fibroblast L929 cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS.Cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells per well and infected with HAdV-3-TZ01 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1, calculated based on TCID50 titers. Following viral adsorption for 1–2 h, the inoculum was removed and replaced with fresh maintenance medium. Mock-infected cells received culture medium alone. Samples were collected at 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-infection for viral genome quantification. Total cellular DNA was extracted using a Universal Genomic DNA Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Viral genome levels were quantified by quantitative PCR (qPCR) targeting the conserved adenoviral hexon gene region using previously described primers (Qiu et al., 2018). Primer sequences are listed in Table 1. Relative viral genome levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method. Viral genome levels at different time points were normalized to the 12 hpi sample within each cell line, which was defined as the baseline level, and normalized values were transformed to log10 scale for visualization and statistical analysis. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn the present study, we isolated and characterized a contemporary clinical HAdV-3 strain, HAdV-3-TZ01. Genomic analysis confirmed that HAdV-3-TZ01 belonged to HAdV-3 and retained the characteristic genetic features of currently circulating strains. Functional characterization revealed robust viral genome replication in human respiratory epithelial cells and multiple epithelial-derived tumor cell lines. Intratumoral administration significantly inhibited tumor growth in an A549 xenograft model, with no detectable body weight loss or overt signs of distress under the experimental conditions. These findings provide updated biological insights into a naturally circulating HAdV-3 isolate and suggest its potential value as an alternative adenoviral backbone for oncolytic virotherapy.The viral genome replication characteristics of HAdV-3-TZ01 were consistent with the known epithelial tropism of species B adenoviruses. Viral genome levels increased rapidly in H3122, BEAS-2B, and A549 cells, whereas replication was substantially restricted in murine L929 cells, consistent with the species specificity of human adenoviruses. Importantly, HAdV-3-TZ01 also showed active viral genome replication in several human tumor cell lines under low multiplicity conditions, suggesting that malignant epithelial cells provide a suitable environment for viral amplification. However, we did not assess receptor expression levels (CD46, DSG2, or CAR) in the cell lines tested, nor did we directly compare viral replication or cytotoxicity between malignant and non-malignant human cells. Such comparisons will be important for evaluating tumor selectivity in future studies.HAdV-3-TZ01 infection induced apoptotic cell death in infected cells. However, the apoptosis analysis in the present study was performed exclusively in 293F cells (a non-tumorigenic HEK293-derived cell line), and the absolute increase in total apoptotic cells relative to mock infection was modest (approximately 4.5 percentage points). Moreover, equal TCID50-based MOIs do not guarantee equivalent viral entry efficiency due to distinct receptor usage, and we did not assess early infection kinetics or apoptosis-associated molecular markers. Whether HAdV-3-TZ01 induces enhanced apoptosis in tumor-relevant cell lines such as A549 or H3122, or exhibits differential cytotoxicity compared with non-malignant epithelial cells such as BEAS-2B, remains to be determined. Previous studies have demonstrated that HAdV-3 infection can activate an intrinsic apoptosis-associated cell death program in A549 cells, accompanied by the release of extracellular vesicles containing cellular stress and apoptotic markers. These findings provide mechanistic support for further investigation of apoptosis-related pathways induced by HAdV-3-TZ01, particularly in tumor-relevant cellular contexts. Most clinically evaluated oncolytic adenoviruses have been developed based on engineered HAdV-5 platforms. Species B adenoviruses, including HAdV-3, utilize distinct cellular receptors from HAdV-5 and may therefore exhibit different patterns of cellular tropism. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of HAdV-3 as an oncolytic platform; for example, the engineered HAdV-3-based vector Ad3-hTERT-E1A showed selective replication and antitumor activity across multiple cancer types while maintaining reduced toxicity in non-malignant cells (Hemminki et al., 2011). However, these studies primarily focused on genetically modified viral vectors optimized for therapeutic applications. In contrast, HAdV-3-TZ01 represents a naturally occurring clinical isolate that showed antitumor activity in vitro and in vivo without prior genetic modification. Therefore, the novelty of this study does not lie in demonstrating that HAdV-3 can infect tumor cells, but rather in providing a comprehensive characterization of a contemporary circulating HAdV-3 isolate by integrating genomic features, comparative replication properties, and preliminary in vivo antitumor activity. HAdV-3-TZ01 is a wild-type respiratory pathogen that retains efficient viral genome amplification in non-malignant bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B); therefore, rather than serving as an immediate therapeutic agent, this isolate provides a valuable starting platform for future genetic engineering aimed at achieving tumor selectivity and attenuated pathogenicity. Genomic analysis identified a short HAdV-7-derived recombinant fragment within the HAdV-3-TZ01 genome. Despite this recombinant region, the overall genomic architecture and major structural proteins remained highly conserved. Whether this fragment contributes to the biological characteristics of HAdV-3-TZ01 requires further investigation.The antitumor effect observed in the A549 xenograft model—approximately 54% reduction in tumor volume and ~50% reduction in bioluminescence signal at day 43—provides consistent evidence of antitumor activity following intratumoral administration. The A549 xenograft model has been widely used for evaluating the in vivo efficacy of oncolytic adenoviruses, including conditionally replicative adenovirus platforms, allowing comparison with previous reports. For instance, studies on the well-known oncolytic adenovirus ONYX-015 have employed this model to demonstrate its antitumor efficacy following systemic or intratumoral administration (Heise et al., 1999). More recently, the A549 xenograft model has also been used to evaluate armed conditionally replicating adenoviruses, such as a p14 FAST protein-expressing vector, which induced widespread syncytium formation and reduced tumor growth rates in vivo (Del Papa et al., 2019). Although H3122 cells showed the highest viral genome accumulation in vitro, A549-Luc cells were selected for the in vivo studies because they provide consistent tumor establishment, reproducible growth kinetics, and reliable longitudinal bioluminescence monitoring. Nevertheless, direct evidence linking the observed tumor inhibition to sustained viral replication and intratumoral spread remains unavailable. Specifically, we did not evaluate longitudinal viral genome kinetics or recover infectious progeny viruses from tumor tissues, nor did we perform spatial analyses of viral distribution through adenoviral antigen staining or functional assessment of tumor cell death by histological markers. These limitations do not negate the observed antitumor efficacy but highlight the need for future studies integrating virological and pathological analyses to define the mechanisms underlying HAdV-3-TZ01-mediated tumor suppression. The dosing schedule employed in this study (two intratumoral injections on days 21 and 34, with a 13-day interval) is supported by precedents in the field, where repeated intratumoral administrations at approximately 2-week intervals have been evaluated in both preclinical and clinical settings. For instance, in the phase 1 BETA prime trial, the oncolytic adenovirus AdAPT-001 was administered intratumorally once every 2 weeks at the recommended phase 2 dose (Conley et al., 2024). Third, receptor expression levels were not examined, and early entry efficiency was not assessed. Fourth, in vivo evaluation was limited to a single xenograft model with intratumoral administration, constraining generalizability rather than undermining the A549 results. For example, CG0070 (cretostimogene grenadenorepvec), an oncolytic adenovirus expressing GM-CSF, has demonstrated clinical activity in patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (Tang et al., 2026). full_text: IntroductionHeat- and moisture-sensitive porous materials such as plush toys, paper products, and foam are widely used in pediatric and healthcare environments but cannot be decontaminated by conventional liquid disinfectants, heat, or UV-based methods. This creates a need for alternative dry, non-thermal technologies. Non-thermal plasma (NTP) offers a promising approach for disinfecting such materials without compromising their integrity.MethodsIn this study, we assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber.ResultsMaterial characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Across all substrates, NTP treatment produced time-dependent reductions in viral infectivity. Maximum reductions ranged from 5.5–6.3 log10 for SARS-CoV-2, 6.3–7.1 log10 for IAV, 4.0–5.9 log10 for HAdV, and 2.7–5.0 log10 for HRV, depending on the virus-material combination. Enveloped viruses (SARS-CoV-2 and IAV) were inactivated more rapidly than the non-enveloped viruses HAdV and HRV, although all viruses were reduced to nearly or completely undetectable levels after 30–60 min of treatment. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic inactivation kinetics characterized by an initial rapid decline followed by a slower phase of inactivation.DiscussionThese findings support that NTP could be an effective, residue-free, and material-preserving method for inactivating a broad spectrum of respiratory viruses on porous substrates incompatible with conventional disinfection. NTP thus might represent a valuable tool for safely reusing sensitive items in pediatric and clinical settings and reducing contamination risks where existing methods are impractical. 2Materials and methods2.1Non-thermal plasma (NTP) deviceNTP was generated by point-to-ring corona discharge in a device whose operating parameters (discharge power: 0.7 W, voltage: 6–8 kV, current: 100–150 μA) were specifically optimized for enhanced antimicrobial and virucidal efficacy. The selected parameters represent the optimal balance between maximum antimicrobial activity and stable, spark-free discharge operation.Further details of the NTP device and the concentrations of long-lived plasma-generated species (NO2, N2O, O3, and H2O2) measured under identical operating conditions were described in our previous study (Bouazizi et al., 2024).2.2Assessment of material damage by NTP using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)Material morphology and surface structure were examined by SEM using a Vega II LSH instrument (TESCAN GROUP, a.s., Brno, Czech Republic) to visualize potential NTP-induced alterations accurately. Small pieces were cut from the samples and mounted on a sample holder using double-sided conductive adhesive tape. All specimens were then sputter-coated with a thin gold layer under an argon atmosphere (15 mA, 60 s) using a POLARON Emitech SC7640 sputter coater (Quorum Technologies Ltd., Lewes, UK). Imaging parameters, including accelerating voltage (kV), working distance (WD; mm), and magnification, are provided at the bottom of the corresponding images in the Results section.2.3Chemical composition analysis of material surface using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed to characterize the chemical composition of the sample surfaces to a depth of ~5 nm using an Axis Ultra DLD spectrometer (Kratos Analytical Ltd., UK). A monochromatic Al Kα (hν = 1486.7 eV) X-ray source operating at 75 W (5 mA, 15 kV) was used, and spectra were collected over a 300 × 700 μm analytical area. High-resolution spectra were acquired with a step size of 0.1 eV and a pass energy of 20 eV. The Kratos charge neutralizer system was used for all analyses. The instrument base pressure during measurements was consistently 2 × 10−8 Pa. Spectra were analyzed using CasaXPS software (version 2.3.17) and charge-corrected to the main C 1 s carbon component (C–C, C–H), set to 285.00 eV. To assess whether the materials themselves affected viral infectivity or cell viability, we tested their intrinsic toxicity toward HRV and HAdV and toward HeLa and A549 cells (see Supplementary Materials). Virus recovery was performed according to the method published in the ISO Standard 18,184 (Textiles—Determination of antiviral activity of textile products, now referenced in the manuscript) (ISO, 2019a), as based on their characteristics, both plush and paper are similar to the fabrics covered by it. For plastic, repeated rinsing of the sample surface, as described in ISO 21702 (Measurement of antiviral activity on plastics and other non-porous surfaces) (ISO, 2019b), would have been sufficient. full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Non-thermal plasma has limited impact on sensitive materialsTo assess the impact of NTP on the structural integrity of sensitive materials, SEM imaging was performed on untreated and NTP-treated samples. Microscopic examination of untreated and NTP-treated samples revealed distinct material-specific behaviors. The paper substrate showed no substantial morphological alterations following NTP exposure when comparing the reference sample (Figure 1A) with the sample after 24 h of NTP treatment (Figure 1B). Plush fabric fibers maintained a smooth surface devoid of defects, fractures, or adherent particles. However, a slight increase in fiber coiling and twisting was observed, which may be related to the localized effects of NTP on surface tension or structural elasticity (Figures 1C,D). In contrast, the foam rubber sample exhibited inherently high porosity, with numerous micrometer-scale particles uniformly distributed across its surface (Figure 1F). NTP treatment did not induce discernible changes in the morphology or abundance of these particles, suggesting limited susceptibility to surface modifications under the applied NTP conditions (Figure 1E). In summary, paper showed no detectable structural changes, plush fabric exhibited only minor alterations, and foam rubber maintained its structural integrity after treatment.Figure 1SEM images of untreated and NTP-treated materials (A) NTP-untreated paper at 2500 × magnification; (B) paper after 24 h of NTP at 2500 × magnification; (C) NTP-untreated plush fabric at 1000 × magnification; (D) plush fabric after 24 h of NTP exposure at 1000 × magnification; (E) NTP-untreated foam rubber at 1500 × magnification; (F) foam rubber after 24 h of NTP exposure at 1500 × magnification. SEM: scanning electron microscopy, NTP: non-thermal plasma.Panel A shows a scanning electron microscope image of dense, overlapping fibrous structures with rough surfaces. Panel B features similarly intertwined fibers but with distinct spacing and visible gaps. Panel C displays thin, elongated fibers arranged in a more open, upright orientation. Panel D highlights comparable thin fibers, some crossing and extending at various angles. Panel E presents a porous network with irregularly shaped holes and interconnected fibrous edges. Panel F depicts a similar porous structure with fibrous walls and cavity-like spaces. All panels demonstrate varying microstructures of fibrous or porous material under high magnification.3.2Superficial oxidation of the material surfaces exposed to NTP analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)3.2.1PaperXPS analysis was performed to quantify the surface chemical modifications induced by plasma treatment. The elemental composition of the untreated reference sample was 58.7 at.% carbon and 41.3 at.% oxygen. Following 24 h of NTP exposure, a clear shift in surface chemistry was observed: the carbon content decreased to 55.5 at.%, while the oxygen concentration increased to 42.9 at.% (Figures 2A,B). This increase in oxygen content is consistent with the surface oxidation of cellulose occurring during air plasma discharge. Additionally, the analysis detected the incorporation of 1.6 at.% nitrogen in the samples treated for 24 h (Figure 2B).Figure 2Spectra of chemical composition analysis of paper surface, (A) unexposed to NTP, (B) after 24 h of NTP exposure. Ref: reference, NTP: non-thermal plasma.Two-panel figure showing X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results for paper samples. Panel A displays the reference paper with C 1s peak deconvolution and corresponding full survey spectrum. Panel B displays paper treated with non-thermal plasma for 24 hours, featuring C 1s and N 1s peak deconvolution and a corresponding survey, where new nitrogen-containing peaks appear. Binding energy is shown in electron volts on the x-axes.The high-resolution C 1 s spectra (Figures 2A,B) were resolved into components corresponding to C-C/C-H (284.8 eV), C-O (~286.6 eV), and O-C-O (~288.1 eV). Furthermore, a distinct signal identified at 289.7 eV was attributed to carbon atoms bonded to nitrooxy groups (-O-NO2). The formation of these organic functionalities was further supported by the high-resolution N 1 s spectra (Figure 2B), which exhibited a prominent peak at 408.0 eV, characteristic of nitrogen in a highly oxidized state within nitrooxy structures.3.2.2Plush fabricPolyester plush fabric exhibited progressive surface oxidation with increasing NTP exposure duration. The elemental composition of the untreated reference sample was 68.9 at.% carbon, 22.6 at.% oxygen, and 8.5 at.% silicon. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study supports that NTP is an efficient and material-compatible method for inactivating a broad spectrum of human respiratory viruses on porous, heat- and moisture-sensitive substrates. By evaluating four epidemiologically relevant viruses—SARS-CoV-2, IAV, HAdV and HRV—across three commonly used materials in pediatric and healthcare settings (paper, plush fabric, foam rubber), we showed that NTP consistently was able to reduce viral infectivity to at least nearly undetectable levels of infectivity after 30 to 60 min, depending on virus–material combinations. These findings expand on our previous work demonstrating the virucidal effects of NTP on surface contaminants, including SARS-CoV-2 and IAV on mask filters and other materials (Obrova et al., 2022; Bouazizi et al., 2024).Material characterization provided essential insight into why all three substrates tolerated NTP exposure without major structural or chemical compromise. SEM analysis confirmed no change in structural attributes at all for paper, only minor changes for plush and foam rubber maintained its structure after treatment. XPS revealed mainly superficial oxidation—manifested as increased oxygen-containing functional groups—consistent with the mild oxidative surface modification described in prior NTP–material interaction studies (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023). Crucially, these observations were made after 24 h of continuous NTP exposure, substantially exceeding the antiviral treatment times (5–60 min), thereby providing a conservative assessment of plasma-induced surface alterations under prolonged exposure. Importantly, no detrimental alterations in material morphology were observed, supporting the suitability of NTP for items that cannot undergo heat-, moisture-, or solvent-based decontamination (Rutala et al., 2023). However, the present assessment was limited to surface morphology (SEM) and surface chemistry (XPS) and therefore could not provide a comprehensive evaluation of the mechanical performance or long-term durability of the tested materials. Regarding the durability of NTP-treated materials under realistic conditions, mechanical properties of paper exposed to NTP under comparable discharge parameters were previously evaluated and shown to remain unchanged even after 120 min of treatment (Scholtz et al., 2023). For plush fabric and foam rubber, our SEM and XPS analyses suggested that plasma treatment induces predominantly superficial surface modifications, which are unlikely to result in substantial changes in mechanical integrity. A comprehensive assessment of multi-cycle durability and mechanical properties across all tested materials is currently in progress and will be the subject of a future study.The differences in susceptibility observed among the four viruses can by some extent be explained by their structural organization and the primary molecular targets of plasma-generated RONS (Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Ahmed et al., 2025). The more pronounced initial reductions observed for SARS-CoV-2 and IAV are consistent with the high susceptibility of enveloped viruses to oxidative damage. Lipid peroxidation and modification of envelope glycoproteins can rapidly abolish infectivity even before substantial genome degradation occurs, leading to steep early declines in viable virus counts (Obrova et al., 2022; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). SARS-CoV-2 was the most susceptible virus, which is consistent with its fragile lipid envelope and the critical role of the spike glycoprotein in host-cell attachment. Oxidative damage to membrane lipids and envelope proteins can rapidly abolish infectivity even before extensive genome degradation occurs. IAV, although also enveloped, exhibited slightly greater persistence under some conditions. This may reflect differences in envelope composition, virion morphology, and the organization of its surface glycoproteins, which can influence susceptibility to oxidative modification (Obrova et al., 2022; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). In contrast, non-enveloped viruses generally depend on the accumulation of damage to capsid proteins and nucleic acids before infectivity is lost, which may result in a more gradual reduction profile (Lion, 2019; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Birmpa et al., 2016). HAdV possesses a highly stable icosahedral protein capsid composed of tightly packed structural proteins that protect the viral genome from environmental stress. Effective inactivation therefore requires the accumulation of damage to capsid proteins and/or nucleic acids, resulting in slower loss of infectivity (Lion, 2019). HRV is likewise non-enveloped and contains a compact protein capsid that contributes to its well-established environmental stability (Wang et al., 2017; Reagan et al., 1981). However, its smaller particle size and less complex capsid architecture compared with adenovirus may facilitate access of reactive species to critical viral structures, potentially explaining why HRV appeared more susceptible than HAdV despite also being non-enveloped (Huang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2017; Reagan et al., 1981). Collectively, the observed susceptibility ranking is consistent with a hierarchy in which viruses protected only by a lipid envelope are most readily inactivated, whereas viruses relying on highly stable protein capsids require more extensive molecular damage before infectivity is lost. Recent plasma-biological interface studies further indicate that plasma-generated RONS and charged particles can act synergistically on biomolecular targets by oxidizing lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids, while also inducing downstream biological responses such as oxidative stress and immune modulation, with the relative contribution of each pathway depending on virion structure (Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Ahmed et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2024).However, the dependence of inactivation kinetics seems to rely on both the material properties and virus type. Beyond the overall reduction in infectivity, the shape of the inactivation curves may provide additional insight into the underlying mechanisms of NTP-mediated viral inactivation. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic kinetics characterized by a rapid initial decrease in infectious titer followed by a slower phase of inactivation. Such tailing behavior has frequently been reported during plasma-based microbial decontamination and is generally attributed to population heterogeneity and limitations in agent accessibility rather than changes in plasma activity itself (Mošovská et al., 2023; Zhang and Wang, 2025). RONS are expected to rapidly inactivate virions that are directly exposed at the material surface, resulting in an initial steep decline. The remaining infectious fraction may consist of particles embedded within surface irregularities, retained in pores or fiber networks, or protected by aggregation and local microenvironmental effects, thereby requiring longer exposure times to achieve non-detectable levels of infectivity (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Birmpa et al., 2016; Mošovská et al., 2023; Zhang and Wang, 2025). full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionRespiratory viruses are major global pathogens because of their high transmissibility, ability to persist on surfaces, and potential to cause epidemics. Although airborne spread is the principal route of transmission, contaminated surfaces and shared objects represent important secondary reservoirs, particularly in communal and healthcare settings (Haas et al., 2023). This risk is especially pronounced in hospitals, daycare centers, and pediatric wards, where high-touch items are frequently reused without adequate decontamination between uses. To address this challenge, the present study examines the virucidal efficacy of non-thermal plasma (NTP), a dry, low-temperature disinfection technology, against four clinically relevant respiratory viruses with distinct biological properties: severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A virus (IAV), human rhinovirus (HRV), and human adenovirus (HAdV).SARS-CoV-2, an enveloped RNA virus, demonstrated remarkable epidemic potential during the recent pandemic (Fathizadeh et al., 2020). Although enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to disinfectants, the prolonged stability of SARS-CoV-2 on surfaces and in aerosols underscores the need for reliable decontamination strategies (van Doremalen et al., 2020). Moreover, repeated outbreaks caused by related coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, indicate that members of the Coronaviridae family are likely to remain relevant targets for future infection-control efforts (Civljak et al., 2020). IAV, another enveloped RNA virus, is a frequent cause of seasonal and localized epidemic outbreaks (Moa et al., 2001). Its persistence in aerosols, low infectious dose, and rapid antigenic evolution make it a continuing public health challenge and a priority target for improved disinfection approaches (Tellier, 2009; Wu et al., 2020).Non-enveloped viruses such as HRV and HAdV present additional challenges because of their marked environmental stability. HRV, a ubiquitous cause of respiratory tract infections, can remain infectious on surfaces and is difficult to eliminate from porous substrates because of its small particle size and structural resilience. HAdV is among the most resistant human viruses; its robust non-enveloped capsid and stable DNA genome make it particularly difficult to inactivate and therefore a useful indicator organism for evaluating disinfection technologies (Lion, 2014; Lion, 2019). Although adenovirus infections are often self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, they can cause severe outbreaks in crowded settings and life-threatening disease in immunocompromised patients (Hiwarkar et al., 2018; Sammons et al., 2019).Standard decontamination approaches, including ultraviolet (UV) irradiation, gamma irradiation, and chemical disinfectants, are often poorly suited to sensitive materials. UV light has limited penetration, and its efficacy is substantially reduced by surface irregularities and shadowing (Deng et al., 2020; Derraik et al., 2020; Kayani et al., 2021; Mills et al., 2018). Gamma irradiation requires specialized infrastructure and may compromise material integrity (Derraik et al., 2020; Rutala et al., 2023). Conventional liquid disinfectants are incompatible with many moisture- or heat-sensitive items and may leave residues that are undesirable in pediatric or clinical environments (Rutala et al., 2023; Obrova et al., 2022).These limitations are particularly relevant for porous, soft, and absorbent materials such as plush toys, foam rubber, paper, and cardboard. Plush toys, often composed of polyester or cotton fibers with sponge-like inner structures, can trap microbes deep within multiple layers. Foam rubber, including polyurethane-based materials used in cushions, child seating, and packaging, readily absorbs fluids and resists complete drying. Paper and cardboard, which are common in books, educational toys, and packaging, may deform or degrade when exposed to heat or moisture (Rutala et al., 2023; Scholtz et al., 2023).Such materials are ubiquitous in pediatric environments, where tactile play, frequent handling, and hand-to-mouth behavior increase the risk of contamination and transmission. Children are also more susceptible to infection because their immune systems are still developing, and viral shedding may be greater and more prolonged than in adults (Costa et al., 2012; Prendergast et al., 2012). Consistent with this vulnerability, contaminated toys and shared supplies in hospitals and daycare centers have repeatedly been implicated in outbreaks of influenza and adenovirus infections among children (Bearden and Casanova, 2016).Against this background, NTP has emerged as a promising alternative disinfection technology. NTP is a partially ionized gas generated at room temperature and atmospheric pressure that contains reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), UV photons, ions, and electrons (Scholtz et al., 2023; Graves, 2012). In contrast to conventional methods, NTP provides dry, non-thermal, and non-wetting disinfection, making it particularly suitable for soft and porous materials that would otherwise need to be discarded after contamination (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023). Previous studies have shown that NTP can inactivate SARS-CoV-2, IAV, HRV, and HAdV on parafilm, P3 R filter material, foam, and other filter-based substrates, with dose-dependent reductions in viral titers (Obrova et al., 2022; Bouazizi et al., 2024).A further advance has been the development of portable, affordable, 3D-printed plasma devices optimized for microbiocidal performance and improved surface coverage of irregular materials such as plush toys and layered foams. By promoting deeper penetration and more uniform exposure, these devices may enable the safe reuse of items in pediatric care while reducing waste, lowering transmission risk, and extending the availability of essential resources during periods of shortage, including pandemics (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023; Bouazizi et al., 2024; Klenivskyi et al., 2024). 2.1Non-thermal plasma (NTP) deviceNTP was generated by point-to-ring corona discharge in a device whose operating parameters (discharge power: 0.7 W, voltage: 6–8 kV, current: 100–150 μA) were specifically optimized for enhanced antimicrobial and virucidal efficacy. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估非热等离子体(NTP)在净化敏感材料免受呼吸道病毒污染方面的有效性,解决对医疗保健和儿科环境中常用的热敏和湿敏基材进行消毒的挑战。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究评估了原型 NTP 装置对四种临床相关呼吸道病毒——SARS-CoV-2、甲型流感病毒 (IAV)、人腺病毒 (HAdV) 和人鼻病毒 (HRV)——应用于纸张、毛绒织物和泡沫橡胶的杀病毒功效。
analysis_zh.methods: 非热等离子体 (NTP) 是通过优化抗菌和杀病毒功效的特定参数(放电功率:0.7 W,电压:6-8 kV,电流:100-150 μA)生成的。使用扫描电子显微镜 (SEM) 和 X 射线光电子能谱 (XPS) 分析材料形态和表面结构。
analysis_zh.main_results: SEM 成像显示,在 NTP 暴露后,纸张没有明显的形态变化,毛绒织物中有轻微的纤维卷曲,泡沫橡胶没有结构损坏。XPS 分析表明表面轻度氧化,没有显着的结构变化。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,NTP 是一种高效且材料兼容的方法,可灭活多孔、热和湿度敏感基材上的多种人类呼吸道病毒,证明了其作为新型净化方法的潜力。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,NTP 可能是医疗机构中敏感材料净化的宝贵工具,为可能损坏这些材料的传统方法提供了替代方案。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究没有提供有关测试的特定病毒株或 NTP 灭活病毒的确切机制的详细信息,这可能会限制结果的普遍性。由于关注的是材料表征而不是直接的病毒灭活测量,因此证据是中等的。

full_text: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025. After 7-day deduplication within the same child, 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included. The NPI period was January 2021–December 2022, and the post-NPI period was January 2023–December 2025. Thirteen pathogen categories were analyzed using period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status.ResultsOverall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher in the post-NPI period (15.2% vs. 6.0%). Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed heterogeneous patterns: human adenovirus showed a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005), whereas human rhinovirus showed a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of human respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting, and data sourceThis single-center, laboratory-based retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Clinical Laboratory at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital of Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital, located in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China. The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. Pediatric respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing records from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Throughout the study period, the data-collecting hospital, clinical laboratory, and respiratory pathogen testing framework remained consistent. Annual pediatric and neonatal inpatient volumes from 2021 to 2025 were obtained from hospital administrative records and used to calculate the number of respiratory pathogen testing records per 100 inpatient admissions as a contextual measure of testing volume across study periods.2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The overall study design, data-cleaning process, 7-day deduplication procedure, study-period classification, and analytical workflow are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Study design, data cleaning, and analytical workflow. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. NPI, non-pharmaceutical intervention.Flowchart of study record selection and analysis. A total of 21,132 pediatric 13-pathogen respiratory nucleic acid testing records were screened; 836 records were excluded during data cleaning, leaving 20,296 preliminary records. After excluding 46 non-first repeat tests within 7 days, 20,250 records remained. These were classified into the NPI period (January 2021-December 2022; n = 6,490) and post-NPI period (January 2023–December 2025; n = 13,760), followed by risk-ratio, interrupted time-series, multivariable, age-stratified, co-detection, and sensitivity analyses.Children were categorized into four age groups: <1, 1–<3, 3–<6, and 6–14 years. This age stratification was selected according to commonly used pediatric respiratory infection epidemiology and the social contact patterns of children in China, broadly corresponding to infancy, early childhood mainly under home care, kindergarten age, and school age.2.3Respiratory pathogen testing and pathogen definitionsRespiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was performed using a multiplex detection kit for 13 respiratory pathogens based on fluorescence PCR followed by capillary electrophoresis (PN: 1060071; Health GeneTech Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China). Nucleic acid extraction was performed using a TANBead SLA-32 automated nucleic acid extraction system. PCR amplification was performed using a SLAN-96P real-time PCR system. Amplification products were detected using an Applied Biosystems 3500 Dx Genetic Analyzer for capillary electrophoresis-based detection and fragment analysis. Sample processing, nucleic acid extraction, PCR amplification, capillary electrophoresis, quality control, and result interpretation were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and local standard operating procedures.The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories: influenza A virus not further classified by this panel (InfA-NFC), influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus, influenza B virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human rhinovirus, human adenovirus, seasonal human coronaviruses, human bocavirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia spp. In this study, InfA-NFC referred to records positive for the manufacturer-reported generic influenza A target, listed as InfA in the manufacturer's instructions, but not classified as influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus or seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus. The seasonal human coronaviruses category did not include SARS-CoV-2. Throughout the study period, SARS-CoV-2 testing, when clinically indicated, was performed through a separate dedicated nucleic acid testing pathway and was therefore not included in the fixed 13-target respiratory pathogen panel analyzed in this study. The Chlamydia category was not further differentiated into C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae. Pathogen abbreviations, full pathogen names, manufacturer-reported detection targets, and limits of detection are provided in Supplementary Table S1.A composite influenza A variable was defined as positivity for any influenza A-related analytic category, including InfA-NFC, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, or seasonal influenza A(H3N2) virus. This composite variable was used only for descriptive summaries and was not included as an additional category in the main risk ratio, multiple-comparison, interrupted time-series, or multivariable regression analyses to avoid double counting. Overall positivity was defined as positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Co-detection was defined as positivity for two or more of the 13 main pathogen categories in the same testing record. Positivity and co-detection rates were calculated using the corresponding number of testing records as the denominator. A 13-target-negative record was defined as a testing record in which none of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was detected. Overall positivity and 13-target-negative proportions describe laboratory detection among tested pediatric and neonatal inpatients and were not intended as estimates of community incidence or prevalence.2.4Study periods, seasons, and school-term statusThe study period was divided according to the timing of COVID-19 policy adjustment in China and the monthly structure of the dataset. January 2021 to December 2022 was defined as the NPI period, and January 2023 to December 2025 was defined as the post-NPI period. In interrupted time-series analyses, January 2023 was treated as the first post-intervention month. Seasons were defined by calendar month: spring, March to May; summer, June to August; autumn, September to November; and winter, December to February. School-term status was defined at the calendar-day level according to the official local school calendar rather than by calendar month alone and assigned to each testing record based on the application date. Each testing record was classified as occurring during an in-school term or a vacation period. This variable was used as a population-level contextual indicator of periods with increased or decreased community contact networks related to kindergarten and school attendance.2.5Meteorological and air-quality dataDaily meteorological observations for Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China were obtained from RP5 (Reliable Prognosis), a publicly available weather data platform providing observational data from ground weather stations. Daily air quality index (AQI) records were obtained from the 2345 Weather historical weather database for Nanchong, a publicly accessible weather and air-quality information platform that provides city-level historical weather records with daily air-quality information (https://tianqi.2345.com/wea_history/57411.htm; accessed July 4, 2026). Before monthly aggregation, extracted AQI records were checked for completeness, date consistency, plausible value ranges, and temporal continuity. Daily temperature, relative humidity, and AQI records were aggregated into monthly means for each calendar month and linked to individual testing records by year-month. Temperature was modeled per 1 °C increase, relative humidity per 10% increase, and AQI per 10-unit increase. Meteorological and AQI variables were available for all 60 calendar months from January 2021 to December 2025 and were matched to the testing dataset by year-month.2.6Statistical analysisAll statistical analyses were based on the final analytic dataset of 20,250 testing records. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges or means with standard deviations, as appropriate. All tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons across the 13 main pathogen categories, the Benjamini–Hochberg method was used to control the false discovery rate (FDR). All statistical analyses were performed using Python software. Data management and aggregation were conducted using pandas and NumPy. Statistical calculations and modeling were performed using SciPy and statsmodels, and figures were generated using matplotlib.2.6.1Baseline characteristics and period comparisonsBaseline characteristics and pathogen detection profiles were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Categorical variables were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test or t test, depending on distributional characteristics. The composite influenza A variable was presented only as a descriptive summary, with influenza A subtypes listed separately. Continuous age is presented as median (interquartile range) and was compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods using the Mann–Whitney U test.2.6.2Risk ratio analysisDetection risks for the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. For each pathogen, positivity rates were calculated for both periods, and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. FDR-adjusted P values were used to assess statistical robustness under multiple testing. As an additional RSV-focused supplementary analysis, age was reclassified into clinically relevant categories for RSV burden and prevention strategies. RSV detection was first compared between children aged <2 years and those aged ≥2 years. Children were further categorized as 0–<6 months, 6–<12 months, 12–<24 months, and ≥24 months. For each category, RSV positivity was summarized for the NPI and post-NPI periods, and post-NPI vs. NPI risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), P values, and FDR-adjusted P values were calculated. This RSV-specific supplementary analysis was designed to provide clinical and public-health detail for the age windows most relevant to infant and toddler RSV prevention.2.6.3Interrupted time-series analysisTo evaluate whether the period difference in overall positivity could reflect a general long-term trend, monthly overall positivity was first analyzed using a single time-trend model without an interruption term. A segmented interrupted time-series model was then fitted using January 2023 as the first post-interruption month, corresponding to the January 8, 2023 policy transition, to estimate the pre-interruption trend, immediate level change, and post-interruption trend change. A joint Wald test evaluated the combined evidence for the immediate level and trend changes, and a grouped binomial model based on monthly positive and negative counts was used as a sensitivity analysis.Interrupted time-series (ITS) segmented regression models were used to assess immediate level changes and post-intervention trend changes in monthly pathogen positivity after the lifting of NPIs. ITS and segmented regression models are commonly used to evaluate level and slope changes after public health policy or intervention changes (21–24).For each pathogen, the monthly positivity rate was used as the outcome. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025. After 7-day deduplication within the same child, 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included. The NPI period was January 2021–December 2022, and the post-NPI period was January 2023–December 2025. Thirteen pathogen categories were analyzed using period comparisons, interrupted time-series models, and multivariable logistic regression incorporating meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status.ResultsOverall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also higher in the post-NPI period (15.2% vs. 6.0%). Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis showed heterogeneous patterns: human adenovirus showed a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005), whereas human rhinovirus showed a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001), with a positive post-NPI slope (+0.64 percentage points per month). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of human respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. School-term status was associated with higher human rhinovirus positivity (aOR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.34–2.52; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002).ConclusionThe NPI and post-NPI periods showed distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection. These findings support integrated hospital-based laboratory surveillance centered on pathogen-specific temporal trends and interpreted alongside demographic, multi-pathogen, environmental, school-calendar, and longer-term temporal context.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting, and data sourceThis single-center, laboratory-based retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Clinical Laboratory at Beijing Anzhen Nanchong Hospital of Capital Medical University and Nanchong Central Hospital, located in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China. The hospital is a tertiary general hospital and clinical teaching hospital that receives patients from Nanchong and surrounding areas. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. full_text_sections.discussion: 4Discussion4.1Principal findingsThis 5-year hospital-based laboratory surveillance study identified marked changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with distinct temporal patterns across pathogens. Overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also more frequent (15.2% vs. 6.0%). At the aggregate level, overall positivity showed a significant long-term increasing trend over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis using January 2023 as the interruption point showed no statistically significant immediate level or slope change. At the pathogen-specific level, ITS analyses revealed distinct temporal trajectories across pathogens, with human adenovirus showing a robust immediate decrease and human rhinovirus showing a significant positive trend change and a positive post-NPI slope. Associations with environmental factors and school-calendar status were likewise pathogen-specific, and phase-interaction analyses further showed that selected associations with temperature, relative humidity, and school-term status differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Overall, these findings demonstrate a complex temporal profile of pediatric respiratory pathogen detection characterized by a long-term aggregate trend, pathogen-specific changes, and associations with environmental and school-calendar factors.4.2Overall positivity, long-term trend, and co-detection across study periodsCOVID-19-related NPIs substantially altered the circulation of common respiratory pathogens (7–11), and subsequent studies reported renewed circulation and altered epidemiological patterns of multiple respiratory pathogens following relaxation of these measures (12–16). In our study, overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period. Further analysis of the overall temporal trend showed that overall positivity increased by an average of 0.49 percentage points per month over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis with January 2023 as the interruption point did not show significant changes in the overall level or trend. These findings place the higher overall positivity observed in the post-NPI period within a broader long-term upward trend and suggest that aggregate measures may not fully capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics across individual pathogens.Co-detection also increased markedly in the post-NPI period, and this increase was supported by both the period comparison and weighted ITS analysis. This pattern may reflect greater temporal overlap in the circulation of multiple respiratory pathogens, thereby increasing the likelihood of detecting more than one pathogen in the same specimen. For hospital-based laboratory surveillance, co-detection patterns provide information beyond single-pathogen positivity and add complexity to etiological attribution and laboratory interpretation. Accordingly, considering both single-pathogen temporal trends and multi-pathogen co-detection patterns may provide a more complete characterization of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity in the post-NPI period.4.3Pathogen-specific reshaping of detection patternsA central finding of this study is that pathogen detection patterns changed heterogeneously after the lifting of NPIs. Although many pathogen categories showed higher detection risks in the post-NPI period, the magnitude, timing, and stability of changes varied across pathogens. This pattern is consistent with reports of asynchronous respiratory virus resurgence and pathogen-specific recovery after relaxation of COVID-19-related restrictions (12, 14, 30). It supports the concept that the post-NPI period may represent pathogen-specific reshaping rather than a simple synchronized return to pre-pandemic seasonality. This distinction is important because aggregate respiratory pathogen positivity may obscure divergent trajectories among individual pathogens.Human rhinovirus showed the most statistically robust trend-related finding in our ITS analysis, with a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption and a positive post-NPI slope. This pattern is consistent with previous pediatric studies showing that rhinovirus activity was less suppressed by NPIs and could remain prominent or increase while several other respiratory viruses showed marked reductions or altered circulation (31–33). The positive association between school-term status and human rhinovirus positivity across age strata is also consistent with evidence that school sessions, holidays, and closures can influence respiratory infection activity in children (20, 34, 35). Thus, human rhinovirus may function as a sensitive indicator of renewed pediatric contact networks in the post-NPI period. Nevertheless, school-term status in this study was defined by calendar timing and should be interpreted as a population-level contextual indicator rather than a direct measure of individual school attendance, classroom exposure, or transmission pathway.Several pathogens, including human metapneumovirus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, and seasonal human coronaviruses, showed immediate level increases in the primary ITS model. Similar post-restriction shifts in human metapneumovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viruses have been reported after periods of reduced circulation or relaxation of COVID-19 restrictions (13, 36, 37). However, these signals in our study were attenuated after FDR correction, indicating lower statistical robustness under multiple-comparison control. These findings are still informative because they suggest transient post-NPI increases for several pathogens, while also showing that not all apparent rebounds were statistically stable after adjustment for multiple testing. For influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, the large period-comparison RR and wide confidence interval mainly reflected sparse detections during the NPI period, indicating a marked post-NPI increase with limited precision of the RR estimate.The RSV-focused supplementary analysis further highlights the translational relevance of age-specific surveillance, consistent with previous evidence that RSV contributes substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children and that RSV activity was altered during and after COVID-19-related restriction periods (2, 10–12). Although the primary age strata were designed to reflect childcare and schooling stages in China, reclassification into RSV prevention-relevant age windows showed that children younger than 2 years accounted for most RSV-positive records and had nearly twice the overall RSV detection risk observed in older children. The highest positivity was observed in the 6–<12-month and 12–<24-month groups, supporting the importance of infant- and toddler-focused RSV prevention and surveillance strategies. The stronger relative post-NPI increase among children aged ≥2 years also suggests broader age redistribution of RSV detection after the lifting of NPIs. Because this study was based on laboratory testing records, these findings should be interpreted as age-specific RSV detection patterns in a laboratory surveillance dataset and may inform future studies that link virological detection with hospitalization and severity outcomes.Human adenovirus showed a contrasting pattern, with both a lower post-NPI detection risk and a robust immediate level decrease in ITS analysis. This divergence from HRV further highlights the pathogen-specific nature of post-NPI changes. This pattern underscores the value of local pathogen-specific laboratory surveillance, because decreases in selected pathogens may be hidden when respiratory pathogen activity is assessed only through aggregate positivity.
