full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionOver 5 years of continuous hospital-based laboratory surveillance, pediatric respiratory pathogen detection showed distinct overall and pathogen-specific patterns across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with higher overall positivity and co-detection rates in the post-NPI period. Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analyses further revealed different temporal trajectories, including an immediate decrease in HADV and a significant positive trend change in HRV with a positive post-NPI slope. Age-stratified analyses and assessments of meteorological and school-calendar factors further showed that associations between pathogen detection, age, and contextual factors were pathogen-specific; phase-interaction analyses additionally indicated that the associations of temperature with HPIV, school-term status with H3, and relative humidity with Ch differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Taken together, these findings support continued hospital-based multi-pathogen laboratory surveillance integrating pathogen-specific temporal trends, age stratification, co-detection patterns, and environmental and school-calendar context to facilitate dynamic identification of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity, prioritization of surveillance targets, and pediatric service preparedness.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionAcute respiratory infections remain a major cause of illness among children worldwide and are associated with substantial healthcare use, hospitalization, and public health burden (1). Among specific pediatric pathogens, respiratory syncytial virus, seasonal influenza virus, human metapneumovirus, and human parainfluenza virus contribute substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children (2–5). Laboratory-based surveillance in China has also shown that pediatric and community respiratory specimens can involve diverse viral and atypical pathogens rather than a single dominant target (6). These patterns vary by age, season, geography, and social contact structure, highlighting the importance of continuous laboratory-based surveillance for understanding temporal changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen activity.During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as mask wearing, school closures, reduced mobility, physical distancing, and enhanced hygiene measures, substantially altered community respiratory virus activity beyond SARS-CoV-2 (7). Observational and pediatric hospital-based studies in China showed broad impacts of NPIs on acute respiratory infections and common childhood respiratory viruses (8, 9). Respiratory syncytial virus-specific studies also reported altered epidemiological and clinical characteristics among hospitalized children during the pandemic period (10). These changes were not uniform across pathogens or regions, suggesting that pathogen biology, population susceptibility, testing behavior, and contact patterns may have interacted to shape observed laboratory detection trends.After the relaxation or lifting of COVID-19-related NPIs, many settings reported renewed activity of pediatric respiratory pathogens, but post-NPI changes have not consistently followed a single synchronized rebound pattern. Studies have described off-season or asynchronous resurgence of influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, and other common respiratory viruses after periods of reduced activity (11–13). Post-NPI resurgence or shifting epidemic features of Mycoplasma pneumoniae have also been reported in China and related pediatric studies (14, 15). The concept of immune debt has further been proposed to help explain heterogeneous pediatric respiratory infection activity after the pandemic (16). These observations suggest that the post-NPI period may be better understood as a phase of pathogen-specific reshaping of respiratory pathogen detection patterns rather than a simple return to pre-pandemic seasonality.In parallel with changes in population contact patterns, environmental and calendar-related factors may provide important context for respiratory pathogen activity. Temperature and meteorological conditions have been associated with viral seasonality and pathogen-specific acute respiratory infection patterns (17, 18). Air pollution has also been linked to respiratory infection susceptibility and pediatric respiratory health (19). School sessions have been associated with seasonal outbreaks of medically attended respiratory infections (20). Nevertheless, few studies have jointly evaluated meteorological conditions, air quality, and school-term status across multiple pediatric respiratory pathogen categories in the post-NPI period.Although evidence on post-NPI respiratory pathogen activity is increasing, the available literature remains constrained by several methodological limitations. Many studies have relied on short observation windows, selected-pathogen analyses, or simple before-and-after comparisons, which are insufficient to separate an abrupt post-policy level change from a sustained change in temporal slope. Continuous multi-year laboratory datasets that span both the NPI and post-NPI periods and simultaneously evaluate multiple pediatric respiratory pathogens remain scarce. Moreover, environmental conditions, air quality, and school-calendar context are rarely assessed within the same pathogen-specific analytical framework. These limitations restrict the ability of surveillance studies to determine whether post-NPI changes represent a uniform rebound or a more complex reshaping of pathogen-specific detection patterns.To address these gaps, we analyzed 20,250 pediatric throat-swab testing records collected over five consecutive years, from January 2021 to December 2025. We compared pathogen detection risks between the NPI and post-NPI periods, evaluated overall long-term and segmented temporal changes, applied pathogen-specific interrupted time-series models, and assessed associations of meteorological factors, air quality, and school-term status with pathogen-specific positivity, including potential variation in these associations across study periods. The study analyzed nucleic acid testing records from a tertiary hospital in Nanchong, China, and found that overall positivity and co-detection rates increased in the post-NPI period.
